newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss hounded for Nazi loot after ignoring past.
newsitem.headline: Swiss hounded for Nazi loot after ignoring past.

text.p: Switzerland, increasingly hounded by claims it hoards Nazi booty, is paying the price for not coming to grips earlier with its World War Two history as a willing banker for any side, historians say.

British allegations this week that Swiss vaults may hold Nazi German gold are just the latest in a wave of allegations the Alpine state may be hiding wartime wealth left by both Nazis and their victims.
Swiss bankers and politicians argue they are now launching serious efforts to uncover lost accounts left by Jews murdered in the Holocaust and trace the murky movements of Nazi loot.
"The position of the government for several months now has been to seek full clarity and openness about these issues," government spokesman Achille Casanova told Reuters.

But analysts say the fact that Switzerland waited until 50 years after the war ended in 1945 has hurt credibility, leaving it vulnerable to accusations of hiding Nazi-era wealth behind a curtain of neutrality and bank secrecy laws.

"They are paying the price now for not coming to terms in the years after 1945 with World War Two," said Gian Trepp, author of a history of Nazi gold dealings at the Swiss-based Bank for International Settlements (BIS).

The Swiss Bankers' Association agreed in May to set up an independent panel with world Jewish groups to look for lost Holocaust accounts, and Berne is setting up a commission to examine the wartime history of Swiss banking.
Former U.S. Federal Reserve Board Chairman Paul Volcker, chairman of the Holocaust account panel, was in Zurich and Berne on Thursday and Friday to begin preparing for its operations, bankers said.
But the bankers and Berne only acted under mounting pressure from world Jewish groups and U.S. and British politicians.
Switzerland never forced a broad public debate about the dark side of its past as a neutral state with strong wartime pro-German elements.
"The job of coping with the war past was not as thorough here as it was in Germany, for example," Guido Koller, historian at the Swiss Federal Archives, told Reuters.
Instead, official Switzerland has preferred to toast the memory of its militia-style army for defending the borders and keeping Switzerland out of the fighting that raged outside.

However, most historians say it was not the Swiss army alone that prevented occupation by Germany, but rather Swiss willingness to finance the Nazi war economy, export technology and allow Hitler to transport war materials through the Alps.
The Swiss government only got around to apologising last year, 50 years after the war ended, for turning back German Jewish refugees from 1938 to 1945 to face death in Nazi camps.
Swiss banks had also opened accounts for European Jews hoping to hide their wealth from the Nazis after Hitler gained power in 1933.
With six million Jews murdered in the Holocaust, there were few survivors left to claim old accounts and few heirs with the kind of iron-clad documents needed to find and claim accounts.
The World Jewish Congress began lobbying Swiss banks last year for a new sweep for Holocaust accounts, arguing a 1960s search that turned up 9.5 million Swiss francs ($7.7 million) was not enough.
Since then, declassified U.S. documents have fuelled claims that Swiss companies hid war profits after 1945.
In response, Berne is drafting legislation to set up a commission charged with untangling the history of the Swiss financial establishment in wartime Europe.

Allegations in a British Foreign Office report this week that Switzerland kept nearly most Nazi gold demanded by the Allied powers after 1945 have added to pressure for the commission to get going soon.
"The government may be embarrassed by suspicions that Nazi gold is bunkered underneath Federal Square (in Berne) and move a little faster," historian Trepp said. ($1=1.2360 Swiss Franc)
